subsystem.name: fault_injection
subsystem.note: The S9/I-11 fault-injection harness, interlock tests/fault_injection/, 5 test files plus the durable modules they drive (contract, controller, manifest + frozen manifest.json, conformance) and two adapters. One ledger per source file. The subsystem is an acceptance HARNESS rather than a product module: there is no claude_org_runtime/fault_injection/, and the port therefore lands in a directory of its own (test/fault_injection/) rather than in src/ -- see DECISIONS.md D-0601, which also records why it is not merged into test/contract/.

file.note: The two-phase barrier protocol and the process hygiene around it -- the portable-lane tests, which run on every OS because a barrier that only works on Linux is a harness that only works on Linux. The inventory is `pytest --collect-only -q` on the source at 65f36c5, in collection order. It was taken under the DEFAULT profile (S9_PROFILE unset, so `fast`), which is why the 98 ids contain 21 manifest cases and not all 59 the frozen matrix holds -- the other 38 are `full`-only and are not collected by a default run. That distinction is load-bearing for this belt's completion claim and is spelled out in the cases ledger.

systematic_mappings.from: a synchronous controller: a reader thread fills a queue and the case blocks on `queue.get(timeout=...)`
systematic_mappings.to: an async controller: the child's stdout is split on newlines by a `data` handler into a pending list with queued waiters, and every waiting method is `async`
systematic_mappings.why: Node has no blocking read on a child process's pipe from the parent side. The ordering property the design rests on is unchanged -- the barrier is what sequences the run, not the timing -- and every wait is still bounded by the same host-monotonic deadline, so a barrier that is never reached is still an attributable failure rather than a wedged job.

systematic_mappings.from: the driver's blocking `control.readline()` inside the barrier hook
systematic_mappings.to: a blocking `fs.readSync` on the inherited control fd in the driver child
systematic_mappings.why: This is the half that must NOT become a poll: the design's claim is that the process freezes mid-window holding whatever the operation script left open, and a spin loop would be a different program. Measured on Node 22.17.0 before the port was written: a 700ms hold consumed 0 EAGAIN retries, so the read genuinely blocks. The EAGAIN arm is kept anyway so a pipe left non-blocking by a future caller degrades to a poll instead of crashing.
systematic_mappings.affects: every case that reaches a barrier

systematic_mappings.why: TypeScript has no context manager. The `finally` is what keeps teardown unconditional (design 8.2) on the pass, fail and error paths alike, which is the property case 10 exists to assert.
systematic_mappings.affects: every case that spawns a process

systematic_mappings.to: `expectRefusal(fn, X, match)` from test/testkit/errors.ts, or `rejects.toBeInstanceOf` / `rejects.toThrow` at the async sites
systematic_mappings.why: The testkit helper keeps both halves pytest asserts -- the class and a regex SEARCH over the message -- one of which a bare `toThrow` silently drops.

Keeps the reason with the result and keeps the mark distinct from `test.todo`. Declared in `approved_non_running` with an exact count, and in `conditionally_collected` because `vitest list` omits a skipped test where pytest collects one.

ids: test/fault_injection/protocol.test.ts::the arming vocabulary > target-only -- a malformed occurrence index is refused at parse, not at a timeout
target_only_tests.why: One, added by the review gate's third round. The source's `int(occurrence)` raises on anything that is not a whole number, so it has the property for free; `Number.parseInt` has neither half of it. It accepts a PREFIX, so `...:2junk` silently becomes occurrence 2 and arms a different pass through the loop than the case declared. And it returns `NaN` for `...:abc`, which slips through the constructor's `occurrence < 1` guard because every comparison with `NaN` is false -- the anchor then matches no occurrence, the barrier is never reached, and the case dies as a CI TIMEOUT. That is precisely what design section 3.1 exists to prevent ('a barrier that cannot be reached is a manifest error, not a CI timeout'), so a parse that can produce it has lost the property the eager parse is for. The case pins the refusals and, on the other side, pins that an EMPTY suffix still defaults to 1 -- the source's documented behaviour, which `ArmedAnchor.parse('lease-acquired')` depends on and which a stricter guard could have quietly taken away.

approved_non_running.reason: The three POSIX-only cases the source itself marks `skipif(not _POSIX)`: two read a SIGKILL exit status, which Windows does not report, and one asserts POSIX sessions and process groups, which Windows does not have (the source's controller carries an explicit Job Object branch there instead). Exactly three, one per source mark; a fourth would need its own approval.

inherited_limitations.behaviour: Node reaps every child process automatically, so the window the source sweeps the process group in -- after the leader is dead but BEFORE it is reaped, when its pid and therefore its pgid provably cannot have been recycled -- does not exist here. There is no `waitid(WNOWAIT)` equivalent and no way to decline the reap.
inherited_limitations.why: Implemented conservatively rather than approximated: the group is signalled only while the leader's exit has not yet been observed, and never afterwards. Signalling a possibly-recycled group is the worse of the two failures. The residual risk is a grandchild outliving its parent -- which the spike driver never creates, because it spawns nothing. The role that does spawn a grandchild is the session driver, and it does not run in this belt. Approved at the human gate for this belt. CARRY-OVER for whoever lands the session lane: if that belt actually runs the session driver, it should decide then whether a dedicated reaper is needed. A dedicated reaper was considered here and deliberately NOT adopted.

inherited_limitations.behaviour: `hardExit` in the driver uses `process.exit`, which -- unlike the source's `os._exit` -- emits Node's `exit` event before terminating.
inherited_limitations.why: Node has no `os._exit`. What the barrier needs is that the stack does not unwind, no `finally` runs and the SQLite connection is not closed in an orderly way, and `process.exit` gives all three; this module registers no `exit` listener, so the difference is unobservable here. The exit STATUS is preserved, which matters because the controller reads it to tell a crash from a clean finish.

inherited_limitations.behaviour: `Controller._remaining` floors every wait at 0.1s: `max(0.1, min(wantS, deadline - now))`. Once a case's deadline has passed, each subsequent wait is still granted 0.1s rather than zero, so a case can overrun its budget by roughly 0.1s per remaining wait, and a role that reports completion just after the budget can still be accepted.
inherited_limitations.why: INHERITED AND UNCHANGED, deliberately. interlock's controller.py line 386-387 is `return max(0.1, min(want_s, self._deadline - time.monotonic()))` -- byte-for-byte the same floor -- so this is the source's behaviour rather than a translation defect, and rule 0 of docs/test-translation-conventions.md forbids a stricter translation. The overrun is bounded rather than unbounded (a case makes a bounded number of waits, and each is still capped by the barrier timeout), the hang protection the design actually relies on is the per-barrier deadline, and `checkDeadline()` still throws `CaseTimeout` outright at bootstrap and at every spawn. Raised as [P2] by the review gate's third round and NOT changed here: removing the floor would make a wait that was about to succeed fail instead, which under load is a false red in a suite that runs `retry: 0` -- and this belt has already observed one load-induced timeout on this machine. Whether to tighten it is a change to interlock's own watchdog semantics and belongs to a decision, not to a translation; flagged to the window with this entry as the trail.

entries.target_id: test/fault_injection/protocol.test.ts::the arming vocabulary > an armed anchor round trips through its wire form
entries.reason: Straight port of the three assertions, with one translation decision. The source's ArmedAnchor is a frozen dataclass, so `ArmedAnchor.parse(anchor.wire()) == anchor` is a VALUE comparison for free. A TypeScript class gets reference equality instead, and an `==` translated as `toBe` would compare two distinct objects and always fail, while `toEqual` would silently stop checking the class. So ArmedAnchor carries an explicit `equals()` and the case calls it -- keeping both halves the source gets for free, and keeping the round trip a real assertion rather than a tautology about identity.

test/fault_injection/protocol.test.ts::the barrier > an unarmed checkpoint costs no round trip
entries.reason: The one structural adaptation this whole belt carries: the source's controller blocks a thread on a queue while a reader thread fills it, and Node has no blocking read on a child's pipe from the parent side, so every controller method that waits is `async` and the case awaits it. Nothing about the ORDERING changes -- the barrier is still what sequences the run and the waits are still bounded by the same host-monotonic deadlines -- but every call site gains an `await`, and teardown moves from the `with` block's `__exit__` to a `finally`. The assertions themselves are the source's, unchanged: no checkpoint event and no sync event in the trace, a done event present, and at least one step naming the attempt operation -- which is what makes 'the windows a case does not name are free' a statement about work that actually happened rather than about a process that did nothing.

entries.target_id: test/fault_injection/protocol.test.ts::process hygiene > every role process gets its own session and group
entries.reason: The property is the source's -- the role process is a session and process-group leader, so a stray shell cannot be confused with it and the group signals as a unit -- but there is no `os.getpgid` in Node, and asserting only the harness's own recorded pgid would assert that the harness agrees with itself. So the group id is read back OUT OF PROCESS from the OS: /proc/<pid>/stat field 5 on Linux (parsed from the LAST ')' so a command name containing spaces or parentheses cannot shift the field index), and `ps -o pgid=` on the other POSIX hosts. Both halves the source asserts are kept: the kernel's pgid equals the pid, and the harness's recorded pgid equals the pid. The spawn uses Node's `detached: true`, which is `setsid` and the direct counterpart of `start_new_session=True`. Skipped off POSIX, as the source is.

entries.target_id: test/fault_injection/protocol.test.ts::process hygiene > teardown runs on the unhappy path and leaves nothing behind
entries.reason: The one structural adaptation this whole belt carries: the source's controller blocks a thread on a queue while a reader thread fills it, and Node has no blocking read on a child's pipe from the parent side, so every controller method that waits is `async` and the case awaits it. Nothing about the ORDERING changes -- the barrier is still what sequences the run and the waits are still bounded by the same host-monotonic deadlines -- but every call site gains an `await`, and teardown moves from the `with` block's `__exit__` to a `finally`. The source wraps the controller in a `with` inside `pytest.raises(RuntimeError)`, which asserts two things at once: the error escapes, and `__exit__` ran teardown anyway. TypeScript has no context manager, so the two are asserted separately and BOTH are kept -- the thrown error is captured and its type and message checked, and the `finally` that ran teardown is shown to have worked by asserting the process is reaped and exited. Splitting them is what stops the translation from quietly checking only one.
